6. Output Analysis

How to draw statistically valid conclusions from simulation output: transient versus steady-state behavior, confidence intervals for terminating simulations, and initial-data deletion, replication/deletion, batch means, regenerative and sequential methods for steady-state parameters.

flowchart LR
    ID(["input distributions"]) --> RV["random variates (rv's)"] --> P["simulation program"] --> Y["output random variables Y₁, Y₂, …"]

The inputs are random, so the outputs Y1,Y2,…Y_1, Y_2, \dotsY1​,Y2​,… are random variables too. A performance measure is a statistic, i.e. a function of the output r.v.s:

h(Y1,Y2,… )  →  performance measure,e.g. h=Y1+⋯+Ynn.h(Y_1, Y_2, \dots) \;\to\; \text{performance measure}, \qquad \text{e.g. } h = \frac{Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n}{n} . h(Y1​,Y2​,…)→performance measure,e.g. h=nY1​+⋯+Yn​​.

Wrong procedure in practice: perform a single simulation run of arbitrary length and treat the simulation estimates as the true characteristics of the system. Why it is wrong:

  • One run gives one realization of h(Y1,Y2,… )h(Y_1, Y_2, \dots)h(Y1​,Y2​,…), which is a random variable: a different seed gives a different answer, and a single number says nothing about how far it may be from the truth.
  • Within a run the YiY_iYi​’s are not i.i.d. (see the example below), so the formulas of §2.6, which need i.i.d. data, cannot be applied to them.
  • With an arbitrary run length, the result can depend heavily on the initial conditions (§6.1).

Q: What is the correct way to estimate the true performance of the system based on simulation outputs?

Ex: queueing simulation. YiY_iYi​ = the delay of the iii-th customer. Lindley’s equation (§2.5):

Y1=0,Yi+1=max⁡{0, Yi+Si−Xi+1},Y_1 = 0, \qquad Y_{i+1} = \max\{0,\ Y_i + S_i - X_{i+1}\}, Y1​=0,Yi+1​=max{0, Yi​+Si​−Xi+1​},

where SiS_iSi​ is the service time of customer iii and Xi+1X_{i+1}Xi+1​ the interarrival time between customers iii and i+1i+1i+1.

The YiY_iYi​’s are not i.i.d.:

  • Not independent: Yi+1Y_{i+1}Yi+1​ is computed from YiY_iYi​. A customer who waits long is usually followed by another who waits long (positive correlation).
  • Not identically distributed: Y1=0Y_1 = 0Y1​=0 always (the system starts empty), Y2Y_2Y2​ is often 000, and the distribution of YiY_iYi​ keeps changing with iii (§6.1).

Solution: perform multiple replications, i.e. independent runs, each with the same initial conditions but its own independent random numbers (e.g. a different stream per run, §3.3).

output process Y1Y_1Y1​ Y2Y_2Y2​ ⋯\cdots⋯ YmY_mYm​
run 1 Y11Y_{11}Y11​ Y12Y_{12}Y12​ ⋯\cdots⋯ Y1mY_{1m}Y1m​
run 2 Y21Y_{21}Y21​ Y22Y_{22}Y22​ ⋯\cdots⋯ Y2mY_{2m}Y2m​
⋮\vdots⋮ ⋮\vdots⋮ ⋮\vdots⋮ ⋮\vdots⋮
run nnn Yn1Y_{n1}Yn1​ Yn2Y_{n2}Yn2​ ⋯\cdots⋯ YnmY_{nm}Ynm​

YikY_{ik}Yik​ = the kkk-th observation in run iii, a random observation obtained from a particular run. Along a row (within one run) the observations are dependent. Down a column (fixed kkk, different runs), Y1k,Y2k,…,YnkY_{1k}, Y_{2k}, \dots, Y_{nk}Y1k​,Y2k​,…,Ynk​ are i.i.d., because the runs are independent copies of the same experiment. So

1n∑i=1nYikis an unbiased estimator of E[Yk],\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_{ik} \quad \text{is an unbiased estimator of } \mathbf{E}[Y_k], n1​i=1∑n​Yik​is an unbiased estimator of E[Yk​],

and the usual i.i.d. statistics (CIs, §2.6) apply to each column.

Idea: use the observations in multiple runs to draw statistical inference about Y1,Y2,…,YmY_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_mY1​,Y2​,…,Ym​.

6.1. Transient and Steady-State Behavior of a Stochastic Process

Output process Y1,Y2,…,Yj,…Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_j, \dotsY1​,Y2​,…,Yj​,… with Yj∼Fj(⋅∣I)Y_j \sim F_j(\cdot \mid I)Yj​∼Fj​(⋅∣I), where Fj(y∣I)=P(Yj≤y∣I)F_j(y \mid I) = P(Y_j \le y \mid I)Fj​(y∣I)=P(Yj​≤y∣I) and III is the initial condition (e.g. the number of customers present at time 0).

The fact that Fj(⋅∣I)F_j(\cdot \mid I)Fj​(⋅∣I) is different for different YjY_jYj​’s is called the transient behavior; Fj(⋅∣I)F_j(\cdot \mid I)Fj​(⋅∣I) is the transient distribution of YjY_jYj​. If there is a c.d.f. F(y)F(y)F(y) such that

Fj(y∣I)→F(y)as j→∞, for all y and all initial conditions I,F_j(y \mid I) \to F(y) \quad \text{as } j \to \infty, \text{ for all } y \text{ and all initial conditions } I, Fj​(y∣I)→F(y)as j→∞, for all y and all initial conditions I,

then F(y)F(y)F(y) is called the steady-state distribution, and Y∼F(y)Y \sim F(y)Y∼F(y) is the steady-state random variable.

This is convergence in distribution (weak convergence, §2.4): Yj→dYY_j \xrightarrow{d} YYj​d​Y. What it means, and what it does not:

  • The limit FFF does not depend on III: every initial condition leads to the same steady-state distribution. But how fast Fj(⋅∣I)F_j(\cdot \mid I)Fj​(⋅∣I) approaches FFF does depend on III.
  • Strictly, FFF is only reached as j→∞j \to \inftyj→∞. In practice there is a kkk such that Fj≈FF_j \approx FFj​≈F for all j>kj > kj>k, and steady state is said to “start” around kkk.
  • Steady state does not mean that the YjY_jYj​’s stop changing or become equal within a run. It means that they have (approximately) the same distribution; they are still dependent on each other.

E.g. M/M/1 queue with ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9ρ=0.9 (arrival rate 1, mean service time 0.9), averaged over 20,000 replications. Started empty and idle, the mean delay E[Yj∣I]\mathbf{E}[Y_j \mid I]E[Yj​∣I] rises from 0; started with a long first wait, it falls. Both approach the same steady-state mean E[Y]=8.1\mathbf{E}[Y] = 8.1E[Y]=8.1, but only after several hundred customers. (The average delay of the first 25 customers from an empty start is about 2.12: a transient quantity, far from 8.1. It reappears in §6.3.2.)

6.2. Types of Simulations

  • terminating
  • nonterminating
    • steady-state parameters: Y1,Y2,⋯→YY_1, Y_2, \dots \to YY1​,Y2​,⋯→Y; characteristics of YYY, e.g. E[Y]\mathbf{E}[Y]E[Y], P(Y>s)P(Y > s)P(Y>s), Var⁡(Y)\operatorname{Var}(Y)Var(Y)
    • steady-state cycle parameters

Terminating simulation

  • There is a natural event EEE that determines the length of each simulation run.
  • Ex: simulate the operation of a retail store over an 8-hr shift; EEE = {8 hours of simulated time have elapsed}.
  • Ex: a manufacturer receives a contract to produce 100 planes; EEE = {100 planes have been completed}.
  • It never reaches steady state, and it does not need to: the run stops at EEE, and the behavior up to EEE, transient part included, is exactly what is being measured.
  • Both the initial conditions and the stopping event should be representative of the real system (e.g. the store opens empty every morning, so each run starts empty).

Nonterminating simulation

  • Any system that operates continuously, with no natural event EEE to stop a run (e.g. a production line running around the clock).
  • Interested in long-run / steady-state behavior.
  • The initial condition does not matter: the steady-state distribution is the same for every III (§6.1).
  • Question: how long should the simulation be performed to ensure that the influence of the initial condition can be ignored? (In the figure of §6.1, several hundred customers.)
  • When the system is cyclic, we are interested in steady-state cycle parameters.

Ex: Y1,Y2,…,Y8Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_8Y1​,Y2​,…,Y8​, where YiY_iYi​ = server utilization in hour iii of an 8-hr shift at a bank (one that operates continuously, shift after shift). The hourly utilizations follow the same pattern in every shift (busy hours, quiet hours), so YiY_iYi​ never settles into one distribution: there is no steady state. Instead, look at whole cycles (shifts):

Yˉ1c=Y1+⋯+Y88  (average server utilization over shift 1),Yˉ2c=Y9+⋯+Y168, …\bar Y_1^c = \frac{Y_1 + \cdots + Y_8}{8} \ \ \text{(average server utilization over shift 1)}, \qquad \bar Y_2^c = \frac{Y_9 + \cdots + Y_{16}}{8}, \ \dots Yˉ1c​=8Y1​+⋯+Y8​​  (average server utilization over shift 1),Yˉ2c​=8Y9​+⋯+Y16​​, …

The cycle averages Yˉ1c,Yˉ2c,…\bar Y_1^c, \bar Y_2^c, \dotsYˉ1c​,Yˉ2c​,… can have a steady-state distribution, and

lim⁡n→∞E[Yˉnc]is a steady-state cycle parameter.\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathbf{E}\big[\bar Y_n^c\big] \quad \text{is a steady-state cycle parameter.} n→∞lim​E[Yˉnc​]is a steady-state cycle parameter.

6.3. Statistical Analysis for Terminating Simulations

Make nnn independent replications of a terminating simulation: each replication starts with the same initial conditions, stops at the event EEE, and uses its own independent random numbers. Let XjX_jXj​ be the performance measure from replication jjj, i.e. a random variable computed from the outputs of run jjj, for example

Xj=h(Yj1,…,Yjm)=average delay in queue of the customers in replication jX_j = h(Y_{j1}, \dots, Y_{jm}) = \text{average delay in queue of the customers in replication } j Xj​=h(Yj1​,…,Yjm​)=average delay in queue of the customers in replication j

(one XjX_jXj​ per row of the replication table at the start of the chapter). Since the replications are independent copies of the same experiment,

X1,X2,…,XnX_1, X_2, \dots, X_nX1​,X2​,…,Xn​ are i.i.d.

Estimating means

Goal: to estimate μ=E[Xj]\mu = \mathbf{E}[X_j]μ=E[Xj​].

Xˉ(n)=1n∑j=1nXj\bar X(n) = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n X_jXˉ(n)=n1​∑j=1n​Xj​ is an unbiased estimator for μ\muμ.

A 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)% CI for μ\muμ is

[Xˉ(n)−tα/2, n−1S2(n)n,    Xˉ(n)+tα/2, n−1S2(n)n ]\left[\bar X(n) - t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{S^2(n)}{n}},\;\; \bar X(n) + t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{S^2(n)}{n}}\,\right] [Xˉ(n)−tα/2,n−1​nS2(n)​​,Xˉ(n)+tα/2,n−1​nS2(n)​​]

(Case 2 of §2.6.1). It is exact if the XjX_jXj​’s are normal, and approximate otherwise (see §6.3.2). Here

S2(n)=∑j=1n(Xj−Xˉ(n))2n−1S^2(n) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^n \big(X_j - \bar X(n)\big)^2}{n-1} S2(n)=n−1∑j=1n​(Xj​−Xˉ(n))2​

is the sample variance of the XjX_jXj​’s.

Ex: ten independent replications of a single-server queue model; XjX_jXj​ = the average delay in queue in replication jjj:

Xj=2.02, 0.73, 3.20, 6.23, 1.76, 0.47, 3.89, 5.45, 1.44, 1.23.X_j = 2.02,\ 0.73,\ 3.20,\ 6.23,\ 1.76,\ 0.47,\ 3.89,\ 5.45,\ 1.44,\ 1.23 . Xj​=2.02, 0.73, 3.20, 6.23, 1.76, 0.47, 3.89, 5.45, 1.44, 1.23.

For α=0.1\alpha = 0.1α=0.1: Xˉ(10)=2.64\bar X(10) = 2.64Xˉ(10)=2.64, S2(10)=3.96S^2(10) = 3.96S2(10)=3.96, t0.05, 9=1.833t_{0.05,\,9} = 1.833t0.05,9​=1.833, half-width 1.8333.96/10=1.151.833\sqrt{3.96/10} = 1.151.8333.96/10​=1.15, so a 90% CI is approximately [1.49, 3.79][1.49,\ 3.79][1.49, 3.79].

6.3.1. Interpretation

“I am 95% sure that [9,11][9, 11][9,11] covers μ\muμ”? No.

[9,11][9, 11][9,11] is an estimate: a fixed interval computed from one set of nnn replications. μ\muμ is a fixed (unknown) number, so [9,11][9, 11][9,11] either covers μ\muμ or it does not; nothing random is left. The formula [Xˉ(n)±tα/2, n−1S2(n)/n]\big[\bar X(n) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{S^2(n)/n}\big][Xˉ(n)±tα/2,n−1​S2(n)/n​] is an estimator: a random interval, because Xˉ(n)\bar X(n)Xˉ(n) and S2(n)S^2(n)S2(n) are random quantities. If the whole procedure is repeated many times (each time with nnn new replications), you get [9,11][9, 11][9,11], [8.5,10.5][8.5, 10.5][8.5,10.5], …, and 95% of these intervals cover μ\muμ. The 95% describes the procedure, not one particular interval.

6.3.2. Quality of CIs

The CI assumes normal XjX_jXj​’s; when they are not normal, the actual coverage can be below 1−α1 - \alpha1−α. To check, use test models whose μ\muμ is known.

Ex: an M/M/1 queue (ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9ρ=0.9, starting empty and idle; XjX_jXj​ = average delay in queue of the first 25 customers in replication jjj):

μ=E[average delay in queue]=2.12.\mu = \mathbf{E}[\text{average delay in queue}] = 2.12 . μ=E[average delay in queue]=2.12.

Construct 500 90% CIs for estimating μ\muμ, each CI constructed based on nnn simulation replications, and count the percentage of these 500 intervals that actually cover μ\muμ.

nnn actual coverage (500 CIs) simulation (20,000 CIs)
5 88% 83.5%
10 86% 85.8%
20 89% 88.1%
40 92% 89.1%

Ex: reliability example: a system of three components that fails when component 1 fails or when both components 2 and 3 have failed; the component lifetimes are i.i.d. Weibull (shape 0.5, scale 1). XjX_jXj​ = time to failure of the system in replication jjj, and μ=0.78\mu = 0.78μ=0.78 (exactly 7/97/97/9). Perform the same experiment:

nnn actual coverage (500 CIs) simulation (20,000 CIs)
5 71% 71.4%
10 75% 75.9%
20 80% 80.1%
40 84% 83.7%

A coverage value based on only 500 intervals is accurate to about ±2.6%\pm 2.6\%±2.6% (the standard error of a proportion near 0.9 from 500 trials is 0.9×0.1/500=1.3%\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/500} = 1.3\%0.9×0.1/500​=1.3%). So the small ups and downs in the first table (88% → 86% → 89% → 92%) are within this noise; with 20,000 intervals the coverage rises steadily toward 90% as nnn grows.

The reliability coverage is lower. Why is there such a big difference?

Fact: the quality of the confidence interval depends on both nnn and the nature of XjX_jXj​. If XjX_jXj​ itself is the average of a large number of quantities, then the resulting CI in general has good coverage.

Why: the ttt-interval is exact only for normal XjX_jXj​; otherwise it relies on the CLT to make Xˉ(n)\bar X(n)Xˉ(n) approximately normal, and the further the distribution of XjX_jXj​ is from normal (especially the more skewed it is), the larger nnn must be. In the M/M/1 example, XjX_jXj​ is an average of 25 delays and is already fairly close to normal (skewness 1.7). In the reliability example, XjX_jXj​ is a single time to failure, not an average: most systems fail almost immediately but a few last very long (skewness 5.3), far from normal.

(The 25 delays within a run are positively correlated, so averaging them helps less than averaging 25 independent values would, but it still helps.)

In the 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)% CI  Xˉ(n)±tα/2, n−1S2(n)/n\ \bar X(n) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{S^2(n)/n} Xˉ(n)±tα/2,n−1​S2(n)/n​:

  • 1−α1 - \alpha1−α is the coverage probability;
  • nnn is the sample size (number of replications);
  • δ=tα/2, n−1S2(n)/n\delta = t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{S^2(n)/n}δ=tα/2,n−1​S2(n)/n​ is the half-width of the CI, because the CI is [center−half-width, center+half-width][\text{center} - \text{half-width},\ \text{center} + \text{half-width}][center−half-width, center+half-width]. The half-width measures the precision: the smaller, the more precise.

If I increase 1−α1 - \alpha1−α (α\alphaα goes down), the tail area α/2\alpha/2α/2 gets smaller, so the critical value tα/2, n−1t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}tα/2,n−1​ is pushed to the right:

However, if ttt gets larger, the interval becomes wider and the precision is lower. If the range is too large, it is not informative: e.g. a 100% CI for a salary is [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞), which is useless.

So for a fixed nnn, more confidence costs precision. The way to get both is to increase nnn: the half-width shrinks like 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​ (made precise in the procedures below).

Var⁡(Zj)=Var⁡(D1)+Var⁡(D2)−2cov⁡(D1,D2)\operatorname{Var}(Z_j) = \operatorname{Var}(D_1) + \operatorname{Var}(D_2) - 2\operatorname{cov}(D_1, D_2) Var(Zj​)=Var(D1​)+Var(D2​)−2cov(D1​,D2​)

drops from 3.79 to 2.23 in this example. Since the required nnn is proportional to the variance (first case), that is about 40% fewer replications for the same half-width.

6.3.4. Choosing initial conditions in terminating simulations

The initial conditions affect the results of a terminating simulation, so they must be representative of the real system (§6.2). In general there are two approaches.

Ex: estimate the expected average delay in queue of bank customers who arrive and complete their delays between noon and 1 pm.

Noon to 1 pm is the lunch rush, so at noon the bank is usually already busy. Starting the simulation empty and idle at noon would miss the customers already waiting then, and would underestimate the delays (as in the figure of §6.1, a queue started empty has smaller delays for a while).

Approach 1: start the simulation empty at 9 am (when the bank really opens, so “empty” is realistic), run the model for 3 hrs, reset the statistical counters at 12:00 noon and collect data for the next hr. The 9 am to noon part is a warm-up that builds up a realistic state at noon; its statistics are discarded.

Approach 2: collect data on the number of customers present at 12 noon (over many days), use the data to fit a distribution, and draw from that distribution to initialize the simulation at noon in each replication; then collect data from noon to 1 pm.

  • Approach 1 needs no extra data, but every replication spends 3 simulated hours only to reach noon, and the arrivals during those hours must be modeled correctly (e.g. with a time-varying arrival rate, §4.6).
  • Approach 2 saves those 3 hours, but needs real data on the state at noon, and the number of customers may not describe the whole state (e.g. how much service the customers already in service still need; for exponential service times this does not matter, by the memoryless property).

In both approaches the replications stay i.i.d.: in approach 2, each replication draws its own initial number of customers independently.

6.3.5. Summary for terminating simulations

  1. We must perform multiple independent simulation runs (replications); a single run is not enough (start of this chapter).
  2. It is important to control the precision of the estimator, i.e. determine nnn (§6.3.3).
  3. Initial conditions must be carefully chosen (§6.3.4).

6.4. Statistical Analysis for Steady-State Parameters (Non-Terminating)

Let Y1,Y2,…Y_1, Y_2, \dotsY1​,Y2​,… be the output r.v.s of a nonterminating simulation. YiY_iYi​ converges to YYY in distribution; more formally,

FYi(y)→FY(y)as i→∞, for all y,F_{Y_i}(y) \to F_Y(y) \quad \text{as } i \to \infty, \text{ for all } y, FYi​​(y)→FY​(y)as i→∞, for all y,

where FYi(y)=P(Yi≤y)F_{Y_i}(y) = P(Y_i \le y)FYi​​(y)=P(Yi​≤y) is the transient distribution of YiY_iYi​ (written Fi(y∣I)F_i(y \mid I)Fi​(y∣I) in §6.1) and FYF_YFY​ is the steady-state distribution.

E[Y]\mathbf{E}[Y]E[Y], P(Y>s)P(Y > s)P(Y>s), Var⁡(Y)\operatorname{Var}(Y)Var(Y) are called steady-state parameters (§6.2): they are characteristics of the steady-state distribution FYF_YFY​. Goal: estimate a steady-state parameter, e.g. the steady-state mean

μ=E[Y]=lim⁡i→∞E[Yi].\mu = \mathbf{E}[Y] = \lim_{i \to \infty}\mathbf{E}[Y_i] . μ=E[Y]=i→∞lim​E[Yi​].

Why is it difficult?

  • Problem of initial transience: E[Yi]≠E[Y]\mathbf{E}[Y_i] \ne \mathbf{E}[Y]E[Yi​]=E[Y], because the early YiY_iYi​’s come from transient distributions FYi≠FYF_{Y_i} \ne F_YFYi​​=FY​. So for the plain average of a run, Yˉ(m)=1m∑i=1mYi\bar Y(m) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m Y_iYˉ(m)=m1​∑i=1m​Yi​, we get E[Yˉ(m)]≠E[Y]\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(m)] \ne \mathbf{E}[Y]E[Yˉ(m)]=E[Y]: Yˉ(m)\bar Y(m)Yˉ(m) is a biased estimator of μ\muμ (initialization bias). E.g. for the M/M/1 queue of §6.1 started empty (μ=8.1\mu = 8.1μ=8.1): E[Yˉ(100)]=4.13\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(100)] = 4.13E[Yˉ(100)]=4.13, E[Yˉ(1000)]=7.30\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(1000)] = 7.30E[Yˉ(1000)]=7.30, E[Yˉ(10000)]=8.02\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(10000)] = 8.02E[Yˉ(10000)]=8.02. The bias shrinks only slowly as the run gets longer.
  • Within one run the YiY_iYi​’s are correlated, so the i.i.d. CI of §2.6 cannot be applied to them directly. (§6.4.2–§6.4.4 are three ways around this.)

6.4.1. Initial-data deletion

Given observations Y1,Y2,…,YmY_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_mY1​,Y2​,…,Ym​ of a run, delete the first lll observations and use

Yˉ(m,l)=1m−l∑i=l+1mYi,1≤l≤m−1.\bar Y(m, l) = \frac{1}{m - l}\sum_{i=l+1}^{m} Y_i, \qquad 1 \le l \le m - 1 . Yˉ(m,l)=m−l1​i=l+1∑m​Yi​,1≤l≤m−1.

The deleted observations Y1,…,YlY_1, \dots, Y_lY1​,…,Yl​ are the warm-up period (the same idea as the warm-up in approach 1 of §6.3.4); l=0l = 0l=0 would give back the plain average Yˉ(m)\bar Y(m)Yˉ(m).

Is this a better estimator? Why? The deleted observations are the ones most affected by the initial condition (Y1=0Y_1 = 0Y1​=0 always, Y2Y_2Y2​ is often 000, …), i.e. the ones whose means E[Yi]\mathbf{E}[Y_i]E[Yi​] are farthest from μ\muμ. If the process is (approximately) in steady state after observation lll, every remaining YiY_iYi​ has E[Yi]≈μ\mathbf{E}[Y_i] \approx \muE[Yi​]≈μ, so E[Yˉ(m,l)]≈μ\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(m, l)] \approx \muE[Yˉ(m,l)]≈μ: the bias is (almost) removed. The price: Yˉ(m,l)\bar Y(m, l)Yˉ(m,l) averages only m−lm - lm−l observations instead of mmm, so its variance is larger. So it is better in bias, worse in variance.

Want E[Yˉ(m,l)]≈E[Y]\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(m, l)] \approx \mathbf{E}[Y]E[Yˉ(m,l)]≈E[Y]. How to choose lll? Trade-off:

  • if lll is small ⇒ high bias (transient observations are still included);
  • if lll is large ⇒ high variance (only a few observations are left).

E.g. the M/M/1 queue above, runs of length m=2000m = 2000m=2000 (bias computed numerically, standard deviations from 100,000 simulated runs):

lll bias E[Yˉ(m,l)]−μ\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(m, l)] - \muE[Yˉ(m,l)]−μ standard deviation of Yˉ(m,l)\bar Y(m, l)Yˉ(m,l)
0 −0.405-0.405−0.405 3.3
100 −0.217-0.217−0.217 3.4
250 −0.110-0.110−0.110 3.6
500 −0.043-0.043−0.043 3.9
1000 −0.009-0.009−0.009 4.7
1500 −0.003-0.003−0.003 5.9

The bias matters more than these numbers suggest, because the variance can be reduced by making more runs and the bias cannot. With nnn independent runs, the estimates Yˉ(m,l)\bar Y(m, l)Yˉ(m,l) of the runs are i.i.d., so they can be averaged and turned into a CI as in §6.3 (the replication/deletion approach, §6.4.2). Averaging divides the variance by nnn, but the expectation stays E[Yˉ(m,l)]\mathbf{E}[\bar Y(m, l)]E[Yˉ(m,l)] for every nnn, so more runs only shrink the CI around the wrong value. E.g. with l=0l = 0l=0, the 95% CI covered μ=8.1\mu = 8.1μ=8.1 in 83% of experiments with n=10n = 10n=10 runs, 68% with n=100n = 100n=100 and 26% with n=400n = 400n=400; with l=500l = 500l=500 it covered μ\muμ in about 93% of experiments for both n=100n = 100n=100 and n=400n = 400n=400. So choose lll just large enough that the bias is negligible. That is what Welch’s procedure is for.

It is very difficult to determine lll from a single replication, because the observations are so variable: a value of lll that works well for one replication may be very bad for another. So Welch’s procedure uses several replications.

Welch’s procedure (for determining lll). Welch’s procedure chooses lll so that E[Yi]≈μ\mathbf{E}[Y_i] \approx \muE[Yi​]≈μ for i>li > li>l. The idea is to perform multiple runs, average across runs and then within runs (over neighboring observations) to construct a moving average process, plot the result and “eyeball” the value of lll.

E.g. the M/M/1 queue of §6.1 (ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9ρ=0.9, started empty), m=2000m = 2000m=2000, w=100w = 100w=100. This queue is very variable: with n=10n = 10n=10 runs the moving average still swings between roughly 4 and 12, too much to see where it levels off, so n=100n = 100n=100 runs were made. 6.4.2. Replication/deletion approach for means

Once a good cutoff value (warm-up period) lll has been determined, the analysis proceeds like the terminating-simulation analysis of §6.3:

  • make nnn independent replications, each of length m′m'm′ and each with warm-up period lll;
  • compute the mean and variance estimates across replications;
  • construct confidence intervals;
  • often, use nnn pilot runs to determine the warm-up period (Welch’s procedure, §6.4.1) and then throw away the first lll observations from the new production runs.

In formulas: from replication jjj keep only the observations after the warm-up and average them,

Xj=Yˉj(m′,l)=1m′−l∑i=l+1m′Yji,j=1,…,n,X_j = \bar Y_j(m', l) = \frac{1}{m' - l}\sum_{i=l+1}^{m'} Y_{ji}, \qquad j = 1, \dots, n, Xj​=Yˉj​(m′,l)=m′−l1​i=l+1∑m′​Yji​,j=1,…,n,

then compute Xˉ(n)\bar X(n)Xˉ(n) and S2(n)S^2(n)S2(n) from X1,…,XnX_1, \dots, X_nX1​,…,Xn​, and the 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)% CI for μ\muμ is

Xˉ(n)±tα/2, n−1S2(n)n.\bar X(n) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{S^2(n)}{n}} . Xˉ(n)±tα/2,n−1​nS2(n)​​.

Why this works: the XjX_jXj​’s are i.i.d., because the runs are independent copies of the same experiment (same initial conditions, separate random-number streams), and E[Xj]≈μ\mathbf{E}[X_j] \approx \muE[Xj​]≈μ, because the warm-up period was deleted. So the XjX_jXj​’s play exactly the role of the XjX_jXj​’s of §6.3, and everything there applies: the CI, its interpretation (§6.3.1), its quality (§6.3.2), and the procedures for choosing nnn for a desired precision (§6.3.3). The correlation within a run no longer causes trouble: it is hidden inside each XjX_jXj​, and only the XjX_jXj​’s, one per run, enter the CI.

The production runs should be much longer than the warm-up (m′≫lm' \gg lm′≫l); they can be longer than the pilot runs.

E.g. the M/M/1 queue (ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9ρ=0.9, started empty, μ=8.1\mu = 8.1μ=8.1) with l=600l = 600l=600 from Welch’s procedure. n=10n = 10n=10 production runs of length m′=5000m' = 5000m′=5000 gave

Xj=6.68, 9.13, 6.34, 10.06, 6.36, 6.90, 6.71, 9.70, 9.50, 5.61,X_j = 6.68,\ 9.13,\ 6.34,\ 10.06,\ 6.36,\ 6.90,\ 6.71,\ 9.70,\ 9.50,\ 5.61, Xj​=6.68, 9.13, 6.34, 10.06, 6.36, 6.90, 6.71, 9.70, 9.50, 5.61,

Xˉ(10)=7.699\bar X(10) = 7.699Xˉ(10)=7.699, S2(10)=2.836S^2(10) = 2.836S2(10)=2.836, half-width 2.2622.836/10=1.202.262\sqrt{2.836/10} = 1.202.2622.836/10​=1.20, so the 95% CI is [6.49, 8.90][6.49,\ 8.90][6.49, 8.90], which covers μ\muμ. Repeating the whole experiment 2000 times, the CI covered μ\muμ in 91.6% of experiments with n=10n = 10n=10 and 93.6% with n=20n = 20n=20 (without deletion, l=0l = 0l=0: 89.0% and 89.2%). The remaining shortfall from 95% is the skewness of the XjX_jXj​’s, as in §6.3.2.

Pros and cons:

  • + Simple: it is the familiar i.i.d. analysis, and the XjX_jXj​’s are truly independent.
  • − Every run has to pass through the transient: n×ln \times ln×l observations are thrown away (here 10×600=600010 \times 600 = 600010×600=6000 out of 50,00050{,}00050,000).
  • − If lll is chosen too small, the remaining bias is in every XjX_jXj​ and does not average out over the runs (§6.4.1).

The second point motivates the batch means method: use one run, so the transient is passed only once.

6.4.3. The batch means method

The batch means method is the most popular alternative to replication/deletion. The idea is to perform one very long simulation run and estimate the steady-state parameters from that single run by dividing the output into batches.

Make one simulation run of length mmm, with mmm very large. Divide the observations Y1,Y2,…,YmY_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_mY1​,Y2​,…,Ym​ into nnn batches of size kkk, so that m=nkm = nkm=nk:

Y1,…,Yk⏟batch 1, Yk+1,…,Y2k⏟batch 2, …, Y(n−1)k+1,…,Ynk⏟batch n.\underbrace{Y_1, \dots, Y_k}_{\text{batch } 1},\ \underbrace{Y_{k+1}, \dots, Y_{2k}}_{\text{batch } 2},\ \dots,\ \underbrace{Y_{(n-1)k+1}, \dots, Y_{nk}}_{\text{batch } n} . batch 1Y1​,…,Yk​​​, batch 2Yk+1​,…,Y2k​​​, …, batch nY(n−1)k+1​,…,Ynk​​​.

(Here nnn is the number of batches, not the number of runs: there is only one run.) Let

Yˉj(k)=1k∑i=(j−1)k+1jkYi\bar Y_j(k) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=(j-1)k+1}^{jk} Y_i Yˉj​(k)=k1​i=(j−1)k+1∑jk​Yi​

be the sample mean of the kkk observations in the jjj-th batch. Then Yˉ1(k),Yˉ2(k),…,Yˉn(k)\bar Y_1(k), \bar Y_2(k), \dots, \bar Y_n(k)Yˉ1​(k),Yˉ2​(k),…,Yˉn​(k) are the batch means. Let

Yˉ(n,k)=1n∑j=1nYˉj(k)\bar Y(n, k) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \bar Y_j(k) Yˉ(n,k)=n1​j=1∑n​Yˉj​(k)

be the grand sample mean. This is used as a point estimator of E[Y]\mathbf{E}[Y]E[Y]. Note that

Yˉ(n,k)=1n∑j=1nYˉj(k)=1n∑j=1n1k∑i∈batch jYi=1nk∑i=1mYi=1m∑i=1mYi:\bar Y(n, k) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \bar Y_j(k) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i \in \text{batch } j} Y_i = \frac{1}{nk}\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i : Yˉ(n,k)=n1​j=1∑n​Yˉj​(k)=n1​j=1∑n​k1​i∈batch j∑​Yi​=nk1​i=1∑m​Yi​=m1​i=1∑m​Yi​:

since all batches have the same size, the average of the batch means is just the average of all mmm observations. Batching does not change the point estimate; it is needed only to estimate its variance.

When mmm is large, the influence of the initial condition dies out: the biased early observations are only a small fraction of the mmm observations. (One can also delete a warm-up period first and batch the rest, as in the figure and the example below.)

If kkk is large enough, then the batch means Yˉj(k)\bar Y_j(k)Yˉj​(k) will be approximately uncorrelated and approximately normally distributed. Why:

  • Uncorrelated: YiY_iYi​ and Yi+hY_{i+h}Yi+h​ are correlated, but the correlation dies out as the lag hhh grows. Two neighboring batches are correlated only through the observations near their common boundary (the end of one batch and the beginning of the next). When kkk is much longer than the “memory” of the process, these are a small part of each batch, so the correlation between batch means is small.
  • Normal: each batch mean is an average of kkk observations; by a central limit theorem for correlated observations, it is approximately normal for large kkk (the same reason as in §6.3.2, where an XjX_jXj​ that is an average of many observations gave good coverage).

For normal random variables, uncorrelated plus jointly normal implies independence. Thus, for sufficiently large kkk, it is reasonable to treat the batch means as i.i.d. normal random variables and construct confidence intervals for E[Y]\mathbf{E}[Y]E[Y] exactly as in §6.3, with the batch means in the role of the XjX_jXj​’s. An estimate of the variance (of one batch mean) is

SYˉ2=∑j=1n(Yˉj(k)−Yˉ(n,k))2n−1,S_{\bar Y}^2 = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^n \big(\bar Y_j(k) - \bar Y(n, k)\big)^2}{n - 1}, SYˉ2​=n−1∑j=1n​(Yˉj​(k)−Yˉ(n,k))2​,

and the 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)% CI for E[Y]\mathbf{E}[Y]E[Y] is

Yˉ(n,k)±tα/2, n−1SYˉ2n.\bar Y(n, k) \pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\sqrt{\frac{S_{\bar Y}^2}{n}} . Yˉ(n,k)±tα/2,n−1​nSYˉ2​​​.

Why not simply treat the mmm observations YiY_iYi​ themselves as i.i.d., and use their sample variance divided by mmm? Because they are positively correlated, Var⁡(Yˉ(m))\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y(m))Var(Yˉ(m)) is much larger than Var⁡(Y)/m\operatorname{Var}(Y)/mVar(Y)/m (positive covariances add to the variance of a sum: Var⁡(Y1+⋯+Ym)=∑iVar⁡(Yi)+2∑i<i′cov⁡(Yi,Yi′)\operatorname{Var}(Y_1 + \cdots + Y_m) = \sum_i \operatorname{Var}(Y_i) + 2\sum_{i < i'}\operatorname{cov}(Y_i, Y_{i'})Var(Y1​+⋯+Ym​)=∑i​Var(Yi​)+2∑i<i′​cov(Yi​,Yi′​), §2.3), so that CI would be far too narrow. In the M/M/1 example below (m=120,000m = 120{,}000m=120,000), the naive i.i.d. 95% CI has an average half-width of only 0.05, while the actual standard deviation of Yˉ(m)\bar Y(m)Yˉ(m) is 0.49: the naive standard error is about 19 times too small, and the naive CI covered μ\muμ in only 9% of experiments. Batching fixes this because each batch mean already contains the effect of the correlation within its batch.

Choosing the batch size. The advantage of batch means is that the initial transient is encountered only once. The difficulty is choosing the batch size kkk (for a fixed mmm, choosing kkk is the same as choosing the number of batches n=m/kn = m/kn=m/k):

  • If kkk is too small, the batch means are highly correlated and SYˉ2S_{\bar Y}^2SYˉ2​ can be a poor estimator. (Positively correlated batch means look less spread out than independent ones would, so SYˉ2S_{\bar Y}^2SYˉ2​ underestimates the variance and the CI is too narrow.)
  • If kkk is too large, there are fewer batches and the variance of the variance estimator is large: SYˉ2S_{\bar Y}^2SYˉ2​ is based on only a few batch means and tα/2, n−1t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}tα/2,n−1​ is large, so the CI is wide and unstable.

A rule of thumb is that there is little benefit from more than 30 batches, but there should not be fewer than 10:

10≤n≤30.10 \le n \le 30 . 10≤n≤30.

Why: M/M/1 (ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9ρ=0.9), warm-up 600 deleted, then one run of m=120,000m = 120{,}000m=120,000 cut into nnn batches; 2000 repetitions, 95% CIs:

batches nnn batch size kkk correlation of neighboring batch means t0.025, n−1t_{0.025,\,n-1}t0.025,n−1​ average half-width coverage
5 24,000 0.01 2.776 1.26 94.2%

20 6,000 0.01 2.093 0.97 93.4%

100 1,200 0.11 1.984 0.86 91.1%
300 400 0.33 1.968 0.71 85.3%
600 200 0.51 1.964 0.58 76.9%

From 5 to about 20–30 batches, the CI gets narrower (the critical value drops from 2.78 to about 2.05, and SYˉ2S_{\bar Y}^2SYˉ2​ is based on more batch means) at no cost in coverage. Beyond about 30, tα/2, n−1t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}tα/2,n−1​ hardly changes any more (it is already close to z0.025=1.96z_{0.025} = 1.96z0.025​=1.96), so there is little left to gain; the further narrowing comes from correlated batch means making SYˉ2S_{\bar Y}^2SYˉ2​ too small, and the coverage drops.

E.g. one run of the M/M/1 queue: warm-up 600 deleted, then m=120,000m = 120{,}000m=120,000 in n=20n = 20n=20 batches of k=6000k = 6000k=6000: Yˉ(20,6000)=7.518\bar Y(20, 6000) = 7.518Yˉ(20,6000)=7.518, SYˉ2=2.268S_{\bar Y}^2 = 2.268SYˉ2​=2.268, half-width 2.0932.268/20=0.702.093\sqrt{2.268/20} = 0.702.0932.268/20​=0.70, so the 95% CI is [6.81, 8.22][6.81,\ 8.22][6.81, 8.22], which covers μ=8.1\mu = 8.1μ=8.1.

6.4.4. Regenerative method

The regenerative method is similar in spirit to batch means. It tries to construct independent replications from a single run, using regeneration points. The difference: batch means cut the run at fixed places (every kkk observations), so the pieces are only approximately independent; the regenerative method cuts the run at random places chosen so that the pieces are exactly i.i.d.

A regeneration point is a random time at which the process probabilistically restarts itself: from that time on, the process behaves (in distribution) exactly as if it had just been started, independently of what happened before. The process between two successive regeneration points is called a regeneration cycle.

Ex: single-server queue. A customer who arrives to an empty system finds the same situation every time: nobody waiting, the server idle, and the customer starts service at once. Everything after that (the following interarrival times and service times) is new and independent of the past. So the arrival times of customers who find the system empty are regeneration points. In terms of the delays, these are exactly the customers with Yi=0Y_i = 0Yi​=0. A run started empty has Y1=0Y_1 = 0Y1​=0, so it starts at a regeneration point.

Suppose the output process Y1,Y2,…Y_1, Y_2, \dotsY1​,Y2​,… has regeneration points

1≤B1<B2<⋯ .1 \le B_1 < B_2 < \cdots . 1≤B1​<B2​<⋯.

At each regeneration point, the process after BjB_jBj​ is independent of the process prior to BjB_jBj​. Let

Nj=Bj+1−BjN_j = B_{j+1} - B_j Nj​=Bj+1​−Bj​

be the length of the jjj-th cycle (the number of observations in it), and let

Zj=∑i=BjBj+1−1YiZ_j = \sum_{i=B_j}^{B_{j+1}-1} Y_i Zj​=i=Bj​∑Bj+1​−1​Yi​

be the sum of the observations in the jjj-th cycle.

In the queue, cycle jjj consists of the customers served in one busy period: NjN_jNj​ = number of customers served in the busy period, ZjZ_jZj​ = their total delay. A cycle with Nj=1N_j = 1Nj​=1 is a customer who arrives to an empty system and leaves before the next arrival, so Zj=0Z_j = 0Zj​=0.

Then

Uj=(Zj,Nj)TU_j = (Z_j, N_j)^T Uj​=(Zj​,Nj​)T

are i.i.d. bivariate random variables: different cycles are independent copies (each cycle starts from a fresh restart), but within a cycle ZjZ_jZj​ and NjN_jNj​ are dependent (a long busy period, large NjN_jNj​, also has large delays, large ZjZ_jZj​).

By the renewal-reward theorem,

μ=E[Y]=lim⁡m→∞∑i=1mYim=E[Zj]E[Nj],for all j.\mu = \mathbf{E}[Y] = \lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i}{m} = \frac{\mathbf{E}[Z_j]}{\mathbf{E}[N_j]}, \qquad \text{for all } j. μ=E[Y]=m→∞lim​m∑i=1m​Yi​​=E[Nj​]E[Zj​]​,for all j.

This is the long-run average cost or reward per unit time: each cycle earns a “reward” ZjZ_jZj​ and takes “time” NjN_jNj​ (counted in observations). Why it holds: over the first n′n'n′ cycles there are N1+⋯+Nn′N_1 + \cdots + N_{n'}N1​+⋯+Nn′​ observations with total Z1+⋯+Zn′Z_1 + \cdots + Z_{n'}Z1​+⋯+Zn′​, so their average is

Z1+⋯+Zn′N1+⋯+Nn′=1n′∑jZj1n′∑jNj  →  E[Zj]E[Nj]as n′→∞,\frac{Z_1 + \cdots + Z_{n'}}{N_1 + \cdots + N_{n'}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n'}\sum_j Z_j}{\frac{1}{n'}\sum_j N_j} \;\to\; \frac{\mathbf{E}[Z_j]}{\mathbf{E}[N_j]} \quad \text{as } n' \to \infty, N1​+⋯+Nn′​Z1​+⋯+Zn′​​=n′1​∑j​Nj​n′1​∑j​Zj​​→E[Nj​]E[Zj​]​as n′→∞,

by the SLLN (§2.4) applied separately to the i.i.d. ZjZ_jZj​’s and the i.i.d. NjN_jNj​’s. E.g. in the M/M/1 queue, a busy period serves on average E[Nj]=1/(1−ρ)=10\mathbf{E}[N_j] = 1/(1-\rho) = 10E[Nj​]=1/(1−ρ)=10 customers, so E[Zj]=μ E[Nj]=81\mathbf{E}[Z_j] = \mu\,\mathbf{E}[N_j] = 81E[Zj​]=μE[Nj​]=81.

Assume we simulate exactly n′n'n′ regeneration cycles. Let

Zˉ(n′)=1n′∑j=1n′Zj,Nˉ(n′)=1n′∑j=1n′Nj.\bar Z(n') = \frac{1}{n'}\sum_{j=1}^{n'} Z_j, \qquad \bar N(n') = \frac{1}{n'}\sum_{j=1}^{n'} N_j . Zˉ(n′)=n′1​j=1∑n′​Zj​,Nˉ(n′)=n′1​j=1∑n′​Nj​.

A point estimator of μ\muμ is

μ^(n′)=Zˉ(n′)Nˉ(n′).\hat\mu(n') = \frac{\bar Z(n')}{\bar N(n')} . μ^​(n′)=Nˉ(n′)Zˉ(n′)​.

This estimator is biased, because the expected value of a ratio is not the ratio of the expected values:

E[Zˉ(n′)Nˉ(n′)]≠E[Zˉ(n′)]E[Nˉ(n′)]=μ,\mathbf{E}\left[\frac{\bar Z(n')}{\bar N(n')}\right] \ne \frac{\mathbf{E}[\bar Z(n')]}{\mathbf{E}[\bar N(n')]} = \mu, E[Nˉ(n′)Zˉ(n′)​]=E[Nˉ(n′)]E[Zˉ(n′)]​=μ,

μ^(n′)→μwith probability 1 as n′→∞\hat\mu(n') \to \mu \quad \text{with probability 1 as } n' \to \infty μ^​(n′)→μwith probability 1 as n′→∞

(this is the calculation above). In the M/M/1 example, the average of μ^(n′)\hat\mu(n')μ^​(n′) over many runs was 6.97 for n′=100n' = 100n′=100 cycles, 7.93 for n′=1000n' = 1000n′=1000 and 8.08 for n′=5000n' = 5000n′=5000: a large bias for few cycles, disappearing as n′n'n′ grows.

(zzz, not ttt: the whole result is a large-n′n'n′ approximation.)

E.g. one run of the M/M/1 queue, started empty, n′=1000n' = 1000n′=1000 cycles (8438 customers). The first cycles were (Zj,Nj)=(77.35,18),(0,1),(0,1),(0.35,2),(30.99,11),(3.07,7),…(Z_j, N_j) = (77.35, 18), (0, 1), (0, 1), (0.35, 2), (30.99, 11), (3.07, 7), \dots(Zj​,Nj​)=(77.35,18),(0,1),(0,1),(0.35,2),(30.99,11),(3.07,7),… Over all 1000 cycles: Zˉ=66.695\bar Z = 66.695Zˉ=66.695, Nˉ=8.438\bar N = 8.438Nˉ=8.438, so μ^=66.695/8.438=7.904\hat\mu = 66.695/8.438 = 7.904μ^​=66.695/8.438=7.904; σ^11=396,988\hat\sigma_{11} = 396{,}988σ^11​=396,988, σ^12=22,976\hat\sigma_{12} = 22{,}976σ^12​=22,976, σ^22=1431.8\hat\sigma_{22} = 1431.8σ^22​=1431.8, so

σ^V2=396,988−2(7.904)(22,976)+7.9042(1431.8)≈123,230,\hat\sigma_V^2 = 396{,}988 - 2(7.904)(22{,}976) + 7.904^2(1431.8) \approx 123{,}230, σ^V2​=396,988−2(7.904)(22,976)+7.9042(1431.8)≈123,230,

half-width=1.96 123,230/10008.438=2.58,\text{half-width} = 1.96\,\frac{\sqrt{123{,}230/1000}}{8.438} = 2.58, half-width=1.968.438123,230/1000​​=2.58,

and the 95% CI is [5.33, 10.48][5.33,\ 10.48][5.33, 10.48]. It covers μ=8.1\mu = 8.1μ=8.1 but is wide. Over many runs, this CI covered μ\muμ in 55% of runs with n′=100n' = 100n′=100 cycles, 81% with n′=1000n' = 1000n′=1000 and 91% with n′=5000n' = 5000n′=5000. The cycles of this queue are extremely variable (most busy periods are short, a few are very long with huge ZjZ_jZj​), so the ratio estimator is biased and the normal approximation is poor unless there are many cycles.

Difficulty of the regenerative method: many processes may not have regeneration points. Even if they do, the expected cycle length may be so large that only a few cycles can be simulated (e.g. in a large network of queues, the moment when all queues are empty at the same time is rare).

Ex: single-server queue regeneration points. Possible regeneration points include the arrival times of customers who find the system empty (above). Two choices that do not work:

  • Times immediately after busy cycles end (the moment the system becomes empty) are not good regeneration points if the time until the next arrival is not identically distributed. At that moment the next arrival is already “on its way”: the remaining time until it depends on how long ago the previous arrival happened, which differs from one busy period to the next. (Only for exponential interarrival times does this not matter, by the memoryless property.) An arrival to an empty system, by contrast, starts a brand-new interarrival time.
  • Arrival times of customers who find one customer in the system are also not regeneration points, because the remaining service time of the customer in service is differently distributed: it depends on how long that service has already been going on. The process after such an arrival is not a fresh copy.

What the regenerative method offers in exchange: if the run starts at a regeneration point (e.g. an empty queue), there is no initial transient problem at all, there is no batch size to choose, and the cycles are exactly i.i.d.

6.4.5. Sequential procedure

A sequential procedure sequentially determines the length of a single run needed to construct an acceptable confidence interval.

Explanation. In §6.3.3 we chose the number of replications nnn to reach a desired precision. For a single long run (e.g. batch means), the corresponding question is: how long must the run be? This cannot be computed in advance, because the variance of Yˉ(m)\bar Y(m)Yˉ(m) depends on the unknown correlation structure of the process. A sequential procedure decides while the run is going. One simple version:

  1. Run the simulation for an initial length m1m_1m1​ (after the warm-up).
  2. Construct a CI from the data so far, e.g. by batch means with a fixed number of batches.
  3. If the CI is acceptable (e.g. its relative half-width is at most γ\gammaγ, as in §6.3.3), stop. Otherwise continue the same run to a longer length (e.g. double it) and go back to step 2.

(The procedures in the textbook are more refined, e.g. they also check that the batch means are approximately uncorrelated before accepting the CI.)

E.g. M/M/1 queue, warm-up 600, 20 batches, start at m=10,000m = 10{,}000m=10,000 and double mmm until the 95% CI has relative half-width ≤γ=0.1\le \gamma = 0.1≤γ=0.1. Over 2000 repetitions the procedure stopped at m=80,000m = 80{,}000m=80,000 (9% of runs), 160,000160{,}000160,000 (41%), 320,000320{,}000320,000 (44%) or 640,000640{,}000640,000 (5%), and rarely earlier. The estimate was within 10% of μ\muμ in 95.8% of runs, but the final CI covered μ\muμ in only 90.2% (with a fixed m=320,000m = 320{,}000m=320,000: 94.8%). The stopping rule is slightly optimistic: it tends to stop at moments when SYˉ2S_{\bar Y}^2SYˉ2​ happens to be small, i.e. when the CI happens to look narrow.

6.4.6. Summary for steady-state simulations

The problem (§6.4): within one run the observations are correlated and the early ones are biased. All methods construct (approximately) i.i.d. pieces and then use the i.i.d. analysis of §6.3:

method runs warm-up i.i.d. pieces CI main difficulty

6.5. Multiple Performance Measures

In practice, we are often interested in several performance measures simultaneously (e.g. the average delay in queue, the average number in queue and the server utilization of the same system). Thus we may construct several confidence intervals:

P(V1∈I1)=1−α1,P(V2∈I2)=1−α2,…,P(Vk∈Ik)=1−αk,P(V_1 \in I_1) = 1 - \alpha_1, \qquad P(V_2 \in I_2) = 1 - \alpha_2, \qquad \dots, \qquad P(V_k \in I_k) = 1 - \alpha_k, P(V1​∈I1​)=1−α1​,P(V2​∈I2​)=1−α2​,…,P(Vk​∈Ik​)=1−αk​,

where VsV_sVs​ is the true value of the sss-th performance measure and IsI_sIs​ is its CI. The question is how these individual confidence intervals affect the overall confidence level:

P(Vs∈Is for all s=1,…,k)= ?P(V_s \in I_s \text{ for all } s = 1, \dots, k) = \ ? P(Vs​∈Is​ for all s=1,…,k)= ?

This is the probability that all kkk confidence intervals simultaneously contain their corresponding performance measures. It matters whenever conclusions are drawn from all the intervals together (“the delay is in I1I_1I1​ and the utilization is in I2I_2I2​”).

If the performance measures (more precisely, their CIs) are independent, then

P(Vs∈Is, ∀s)=∏s=1kP(Vs∈Is)=(1−α1)(1−α2)⋯(1−αk).P(V_s \in I_s,\ \forall s) = \prod_{s=1}^k P(V_s \in I_s) = (1 - \alpha_1)(1 - \alpha_2)\cdots(1 - \alpha_k) . P(Vs​∈Is​, ∀s)=s=1∏k​P(Vs​∈Is​)=(1−α1​)(1−α2​)⋯(1−αk​).

E.g. three independent 95% CIs: 0.953=0.8570.95^3 = 0.8570.953=0.857, so all three are correct together only with probability 85.7%, not 95%.

In practice, however, performance measures are unlikely to be independent (they are computed from the same simulation runs). A conservative approach uses Bonferroni’s inequality, which holds for any dependence:

P(Vs∈Is, ∀s)=P(V1∈I1∩V2∈I2∩⋯∩Vk∈Ik)=1−P(V1∉I1∪V2∉I2∪⋯∪Vk∉Ik)≥1−∑s=1kP(Vs∉Is)≥1−∑s=1kαs.\begin{aligned} P(V_s \in I_s,\ \forall s) &= P(V_1 \in I_1 \cap V_2 \in I_2 \cap \cdots \cap V_k \in I_k) \\ &= 1 - P(V_1 \notin I_1 \cup V_2 \notin I_2 \cup \cdots \cup V_k \notin I_k) \\ &\ge 1 - \sum_{s=1}^k P(V_s \notin I_s) \\ &\ge 1 - \sum_{s=1}^k \alpha_s . \end{aligned} P(Vs​∈Is​, ∀s)​=P(V1​∈I1​∩V2​∈I2​∩⋯∩Vk​∈Ik​)=1−P(V1​∈/I1​∪V2​∈/I2​∪⋯∪Vk​∈/Ik​)≥1−s=1∑k​P(Vs​∈/Is​)≥1−s=1∑k​αs​.​

Step by step:

  1. “All intervals are correct” is the intersection of the events {Vs∈Is}\{V_s \in I_s\}{Vs​∈Is​}.
  2. Complement: its opposite, “at least one interval is wrong”, is the union of the events {Vs∉Is}\{V_s \notin I_s\}{Vs​∈/Is​} (De Morgan’s law), so P(all correct)=1−P(at least one wrong)P(\text{all correct}) = 1 - P(\text{at least one wrong})P(all correct)=1−P(at least one wrong).
  3. Union bound (Boole’s inequality): P(A1∪⋯∪Ak)≤∑sP(As)P(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_k) \le \sum_s P(A_s)P(A1​∪⋯∪Ak​)≤∑s​P(As​), because the sum counts the overlaps of the events more than once. Subtracting a larger number gives “≥\ge≥”.
  4. Each interval is wrong with probability P(Vs∉Is)=αsP(V_s \notin I_s) = \alpha_sP(Vs​∈/Is​)=αs​ (at most αs\alpha_sαs​ when the CI is approximate).

Therefore, the overall confidence level is at least

100(1−∑s=1kαs)%.100\left(1 - \sum_{s=1}^k \alpha_s\right)\% . 100(1−s=1∑k​αs​)%.

E.g. three 95% CIs: overall at least 100(1−3×0.05)%=85%100(1 - 3 \times 0.05)\% = 85\%100(1−3×0.05)%=85% (compare 85.7% in the independent case). In the other direction, to get an overall level of at least 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\%100(1−α)%, choose the αs\alpha_sαs​’s so that ∑sαs=α\sum_s \alpha_s = \alpha∑s​αs​=α, e.g. αs=α/k\alpha_s = \alpha/kαs​=α/k: for k=2k = 2k=2 measures and overall 90%, make two 95% CIs; for k=5k = 5k=5 and overall 90%, five 98% CIs. The price is that each individual CI is wider (a larger critical value tαs/2, n−1t_{\alpha_s/2,\,n-1}tαs​/2,n−1​), so with many measures the individual CIs can become too wide to be useful.
